problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(3,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/b7c2c6f9e50988629007a06213cb3acf0a48f9951f026fb70d5a986b760abdfe.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
